docs.title: Welcome to My Research Page
docs.text:
I'm a PhD candidate at the McGill University department of Physics and the Trottier Space Institute. I'm interested in all things gravitational-waves, whether they be from mergers of black holes and neutrons stars, core-collapse supernovae, or spinning pulsars!

My current research involves using machine learning techniques to make rapid predictions for LIGO-Virgo candidate gravitational-wave events. On this website you can read more about my research, including info on projects I work on, and some more info about me.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: I completed my BSc in physics and astronomy at the University of British Columbia, Vancouver in 2019, followed by an MSc in astronomy in 2021 supervised by Prof. Jess McIver. My masters thesis focussed on studying gravitational-waves from core-collapse supernovae. In 2022 I moved to Montreal for my PhD in physics at McGill University with Prof. Daryl Haggard. My work focuses on leveraging machine learning techniques to enable multi-messenger observations of gravitational-wave events.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: I am currently working on the GWSkyNet-Multi project.

docs.title: GWSkyNet-Multi
docs.text:
GWSkyNet-Multi II is a multi-class neural network model developed for the classification of candidate gravitational-wave events detected by the LIGO and Virgo observatories.

The model uses limited information released in the low-latency public alerts to produce prediction probabilities indicating whether an event is a merger of two black holes (BBH), a merger of a neutron star and a black hole (NSBH), a merger of two neutron stars (BNS), or a non-astrophysical transient noise known as a glitch. This classification facilitates time-sensitive decisions about whether to perform electromagnetic follow-up of candidate events during LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observing runs.

The details of the GWSkyNet-Multi II model can be found in Raza et al. (2025). Details of earlier versions of the model and its inner workings are described in Abbott et al. (2022) and Raza et al. (2024).

docs.title: Research Interests
docs.text: I work at the intersection of machine learning and gravitational-wave astronomy. The type of astrophysical sources I study are core-collapse supernovae and mergers of dense compact objects like neutron stars and black holes. I've worked extensively with neural networks to build models that can enable the study of these sources, and am particularly interested in the interpretably of these ML models.

docs.title: Multiwavelength Paper
docs.text:
In this multiwavelength paper, I use data from VERITAS, Swift and CHIME, to study the equivalencies of sample galaxies when investigating instrumental systematic. Applying Keeler's theorem (see also) it can be shown that convergence is quickly obtained, requiring at minimum two additional sample galaxies.
